reference.source: Congenital heart disease references / cardiology guidelines
clinicalPearls: A narrowing of the aorta, typically just distal to the left subclavian artery near the ductal insertion
Presents in neonates with collapse as the duct closes, or later with hypertension and reduced leg pulses
The classic sign is radio-femoral delay with upper-limb hypertension and weak, delayed femoral pulses
Rib notching from collateral vessels and a figure-of-three aortic contour may be seen on imaging in older children and adults
It is strongly associated with bicuspid aortic valve and with Turner syndrome
Duct-dependent neonatal presentations require prostaglandin to maintain the duct before repair
reference.pathophysiology: Coarctation is a discrete narrowing of the aortic lumen, usually in the juxtaductal region, that obstructs systemic outflow. In duct-dependent neonates, closure of the arterial duct unmasks severe obstruction, causing left ventricular failure and shock. In those presenting later, chronic obstruction drives upper-body hypertension and the development of collateral arteries bypassing the narrowing, while the left ventricle hypertrophies against the increased afterload. Associated bicuspid aortic valve and aortopathy contribute to long-term risk.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of neonatal collapse (sepsis, metabolic, other duct-dependent lesions)
additionalInvestigations: Four-limb blood pressure and pulse assessment
Echocardiography to define the coarctation and associated lesions
CT or MR angiography for anatomy and collaterals
Assessment for bicuspid aortic valve and Turner syndrome
redFlags: Neonatal collapse as the duct closes
Severe upper-limb hypertension or heart failure
Features suggesting aortic aneurysm or dissection in adults
reference.prognosis: With timely repair prognosis is good, but lifelong follow-up is needed for recoarctation, persistent or recurrent hypertension, and aortopathy-related complications.
pitfalls: Missing the diagnosis by not checking femoral pulses and leg blood pressure
Failing to start prostaglandin in a collapsing duct-dependent neonate
Assuming cure after repair and not monitoring for recoarctation and hypertension
management: Prostaglandin infusion to maintain ductal patency in duct-dependent neonatal presentations, with resuscitation of left ventricular failure and shock before repair.
Relief of the narrowing by surgical repair in neonates and infants, or by balloon angioplasty with stent implantation in older children and adults.
Blood-pressure control with antihypertensive agents, as hypertension may persist or recur despite anatomical repair.
Evaluation and management of associated bicuspid aortic valve and aortopathy.
Lifelong follow-up for recoarctation, recurrent hypertension and aneurysm formation at the repair site.
Investigation for Turner syndrome and other recognised associations.
Specialist congenital cardiology surveillance with awareness of endocarditis risk.
